messages.author: 291685fb69362edf
messages.subject: Differences across subgroup analyses
parts:
Hi Chris

I happen to have a brief question re. the graphs that are generated by the Braingraph function. I have a number of subgroup analyses I have run (each against controls) and have generated graphs across a large number of densities (.01-.5). I have then used the g[[1]][[N]]$conn.comp (for N=1,2,...49) to assess the lowest density at which the graph is fully connected, that is the density at which the conn.comp attribute returns a value of a single component. However, even thought the same group of controls were used for each sub-group analysis, the density at which the graph was fully connected varied, from 14-16%. 

My question is, what is the reasoning behind these differences? I was wondering if there were any randomization functionsinvolved creating this variability?

BW
Dan

messages.author: dadcb4fd6a01f8d1
messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Differences across subgroup analyses
parts:
What modality is your data (thickness, DTI, etc.)?
Regardless of the type of data, if you created the data tables then you should be able to figure out the lowest density at which the graph is fully connected using the following code: (or some variation)

kNumVertices <- vcount(g[[1]][[1]])    % or kNumVertices <- nrow(atlas)  where you substitute "atlas" with the name of the atlas you're using
dt.G[Group == 'Control', .SD[max.comp == kNumVertices, density]][1]

The "[1]" at the end returns the first value that is output. Assuming the data table is ordered by density.

But to answer your question: I don't know, I would have to see your data. There is no randomness in calculating the connected components.

messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Differences across subgroup analyses
parts:
Could you tell me what the contrasts are representing? I don't see why there would be differences when looking at different group combinations.

To explain the workflow that I have used for thickness data:
1) Import thickness files for *all* subjects, one file for each hemisphere. This comes from Freesurfer's "aparcstats2table" but should work with data from other software if the format is the same.
2) For each brain region, get linear model residuals. I do this for each group *separately*. Perhaps you are seeing differences if you are running one model for all subjects? This would explain why different combinations of groups result in different connected components. (I actually am relatively unhappy with "get.resid" function as it is one of the older ones and would like to re-work it at some point).
3) Correlate the LM residuals for each group *separately*, and apply a series of thresholds to binarize the connectivity matrices. This will result in e.g. 15 graphs *per group*.
4) Create the graphs for each threshold/density and each group.
5) Calculated connected components (and all other measures).

The "dt.G" object was formerly called "dt.global" in my User Guide; it is simply a "data.table" that is created from the function "graph_attr_dt". You can see some code for creating it in Chapter 5.1 of the User Guide. Here are the first few lines of the table for some of my data:

Sorry for the formatting. "max.comp" is the 9th column here and (as expected) increases as the graph density increases.

Hi Chris, So one group represents the control group and the remaining groups are a sub group of the original patient group. 

In terms of your workflow:
1) Import thickness files for *all* subjects, one file for each hemisphere. This comes from Freesurfer's "aparcstats2table" but should work with data from other software if the format is the same.
Done, results in all subjects being read into a single all.dat ad all.dat.tidy data object

2) For each brain region, get linear model residuals. I do this for each group *separately*. Perhaps you are seeing differences if you are running one model for all subjects? This would explain why different combinations of groups result in different connected components. (I actually am relatively unhappy with "get.resid" function as it is one of the older ones and would like to re-work it at some point).

I run this as per the guide, excluding the group variable from the covars table in order to run individual linear models for each of the group. In my covars file groups are listed using group names (i.e control or patient) rather than numerically coded. The formula returned as being used for the linear model fitting is : value~ Sex+Age_scanning+eTIV (eTIV is estimated total intracranial volume as outputted by freesurfer and is only used in the violume not CT analyses)
3) Correlate the LM residuals for each group *separately*, and apply a series of thresholds to binarize the connectivity matrices. This will result in e.g. 15 graphs *per group*.

As per the user guide section 4.5 I have used the corrs <- lapply(groups, function(x) lapply(densities, function(y) corr.matrix(resids.all[x], density=y))) to ensure that the individual groups are correlated seperately. Then I use the graph creation steps in your user guide to finish the process. I assume this is working correctly as I can access two separate graph objects following this.

4) Create the graphs for each threshold/density and each group.
5) Calculated connected components (and all other measures).

Sorry In my saved scripts I was still using the dt.global notation. I have used the code you suggested to generate the lowest fully connected density values and, as expected, this produces the same results as using the conn.comp data (although is significantly easier!!!)

Where would it be best to send some information off-list, is there an email address you would prefer?

Cheers and thanks again,
Dan

On Tuesday, March 28, 2017 at 6:15:18 PM UTC+1, Chris Watson wrote:
What modality is your data (thickness, DTI, etc.)?
Regardless of the type of data, if you created the data tables then you should be able to figure out the lowest density at which the graph is fully connected using the following code: (or some variation)

kNumVertices <- vcount(g[[1]][[1]])    % or kNumVertices <- nrow(atlas)  where you substitute "atlas" with the name of the atlas you're using
dt.G[Group == 'Control', .SD[max.comp == kNumVertices, density]][1]

The "[1]" at the end returns the first value that is output. Assuming the data table is ordered by density.

But to answer your question: I don't know, I would have to see your data. There is no randomness in calculating the connected components.
